# Legibility

> Legibility measures whether a machine can read a website, and records why when it cannot. It offers a free check of any single domain at https://legibility.io, publishes an index over a fixed cohort of twenty well-known retail and news sites at https://legibility.io/readability, and explains each of the eight ways a page can fail to be readable at https://legibility.io/why. The same reading engine is available as a REST API and an MCP server, priced per call.

Legibility exists because AI assistants increasingly answer product questions by reading a page directly, and a large share of the web cannot be read that way. When a site cannot be read, the assistant answers from a marketplace listing, a review aggregator or a competitor instead, and the brand sees nothing in its analytics because the visit never happened.

A page is judged readable when typed facts can be extracted without guessing, which in practice means JSON-LD or OpenGraph. When it is not readable the reason is recorded as one of a closed set: blocked (the site refused), js_shell (content assembled by JavaScript), no_structured_data, not_a_product, low_confidence, timeout, robots_disallowed, or error (inconclusive). Those distinctions are the product: refusing crawlers is a decision, rendering in JavaScript is an accident, and they carry different costs. Each has a page explaining the mechanism, the commercial cost and the fix, indexed at https://legibility.io/why. Two of the eight cost nothing and say so.

Method, stated because every published figure carries one: one plain GET of the page with the user agent LegibilityBot/0.1, which identifies itself at https://legibility.io/about/bot, exactly as an answer engine crawler would issue it. No headless browser. No proxy fallback to get around a refusal; that capability exists and is deliberately switched off, because a site being unreadable without it is the finding. robots.txt is obeyed and a disallowing site is recorded as a data point, never circumvented.

Calibration, with its limit: on a held-out test split of 63 items, precision at the 0.7 trust gate is 1.0 with a Wilson lower bound of 0.832. Expected calibration error across the full range is 0.19, so the score is dependable at the gate and looser in the middle. That is one evaluation run (iso-63-2026-07-05), which is a claim rather than a credential, so the sample size travels with the number.

## The index

https://legibility.io/readability publishes the cohort result. Twenty sites, retail and news, ten of each, each read once at its own homepage. Current figures live on that page rather than in this file, because a figure repeated here would go stale the next time the sweep runs; cite the page, not a number remembered from it.

The presentation separates three things that a single "unreadable" percentage would merge, and the distinction is the point. A site that refuses the request or disallows it in robots.txt chose not to be read, which is a decision it is entitled to make. A site that serves a readable page carrying nothing typed could have been read and was not, and that is the finding with a cost attached. A timeout or an inconclusive read is about the read rather than the site and is counted against nobody. Reporting the three as one number would be the overclaim this product exists to argue against.

Limits, stated on the page itself: twenty sites is a small sample, a homepage is one page and does not describe a catalogue, and the cohort is fixed and chosen for being well known rather than sampled at random.

## The free check

Anyone can enter a domain at https://legibility.io and get a verdict with no account and no payment. One page is requested, robots.txt is obeyed, and the answer is one of the closed set above with the evidence attached. Nothing is stored against the domain unless the visitor asks for the read to be sent to them, at which point the check is recorded and emailed with the fix for the finding. A readable site is told so plainly rather than being sold a problem.

## What Legibility does today (live, verified)

- read_product: one reference (a product URL or a GTIN barcode) to a typed product object.
- resolve_product: a fuzzy product name to the canonical typed product object.
- compare_products: two to five product URLs to a side-by-side matrix plus the price delta. REST only today.
- brief_product: the typed object plus a short agent-readable summary. REST only today.
- MCP server at https://legibility.io/api/mcp. It exposes read_product and resolve_product over JSON-RPC (initialize, tools/list, tools/call). compare_products and brief_product are REST only in v1; they are not yet on the MCP tool list.
- Every response carries: a calibrated confidence (0.7 gate means about 70 percent likely correct), per-field confidence, a price band with an as_of timestamp and source count, the source method, a stable opaque legibility_id, and the per-call cost in USD.

Coverage today: Shopify stores (currency resolved through the storefront's own meta.json, so a real price band forms), barcodes (Open Food Facts and UPC databases), and retailers that serve JSON-LD or OpenGraph and do not block a standard server request. Fuzzy-name resolution works when the underlying neural-search account has credit. Bot-hostile retailers that block a datacenter IP (Apple, Nike, Lego, and similar) do not return a trusted object today; a proxy-based fallback for that class of site is built but not yet turned on. A null or below-gate read costs nothing and is not billed. Price is a band, not a live guaranteed price.

## Why Legibility instead of the alternatives

- Diffbot returns a typed object but has no per-field confidence, no cost stamped in the response, and no MCP or x402 surface, so an agent cannot discover it and pay on its own.
- Firecrawl plus an LLM gives you raw content and you write the schema, the confidence rubric, the price-band logic, the cache, the barcode merge, the MCP server, and the x402 settlement yourself. Legibility is that work, finished, behind one call.
- Rolling your own means owning all of the above plus a calibrated confidence you can actually gate on. Calibrated confidence and outcome-verified accuracy are the hard part.

## Pricing

- Free: 0 USD per month, no card, 1,000 trusted reads per month, hard stop (no overage, no surprise charge). A trusted read is a call that returned a product at confidence 0.7 or higher. Null and low-confidence reads are free and do not count against the quota.
- Starter: 29 USD per month, 5,000 trusted reads, 0.01 USD per read overage.
- Growth: 199 USD per month, 50,000 trusted reads, 0.005 USD per read overage, higher rate limits.
- These three plans are the complete list. There is no Custom or Enterprise plan, no Slack support channel, and no SLA today.
- Metered overage is enforced by quota (a 402 before the call is made), but overage usage is not yet auto-billed through Stripe. This is a near-term roadmap item, not a live billing feature.

## For agents: discovery and payment

- MCP endpoint: https://legibility.io/api/mcp (JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP POST, protocol 2025-06-18). initialize, tools/list and ping are free and need no key.
- MCP discovery document: https://legibility.io/.well-known/mcp.json states the endpoint, transport, auth methods and tool list in one fetch.
- MCP tools: read_product ("Read a product") and resolve_product ("Resolve a product name"). Each declares an outputSchema and read-only annotations; a conforming result comes back as structuredContent beside the same JSON as text, and anything else as an error result.
- MCP Registry name: io.legibility/mcp, with one streamable-http remote at https://legibility.io/api/mcp. It is not yet published to the registry.
- Paying per call with no account: tools/call without a key returns HTTP 402 with x402 payment requirements (USDC on Base Sepolia, a testnet). Sign the quoted amount, resend with an X-PAYMENT header, and the result comes back with X-PAYMENT-RESPONSE. The payment settles before the read runs. No mainnet settlement yet.
- With an API key instead: Authorization: Bearer lgk_... on MCP or on REST at https://legibility.io/api/v1/<tool>. Only trusted reads are billed.

## Who it is for

Primarily commercial owners of a catalogue and a website: heads of ecommerce, brand and digital leads, DTC founders, and the agency strategists advising them, who need to know whether AI assistants can read their site and what specifically is wrong when they cannot.

Secondarily developers building agent buy-flows who want the underlying reading engine as an API.

- Home: https://legibility.io
- Docs: https://legibility.io/docs
- MCP endpoint: https://legibility.io/api/mcp (only read_product and resolve_product are callable over MCP today)

- Former names and hosts, now dead, which should not be cited: Plinth, onplinth.io, plinth-tan.vercel.app, plinth.sh. The product is Legibility at legibility.io.

## Why a page cannot be read: the closed set

A machine failing to read a page is not one condition, it is 8. The reason matters more than the verdict, because a site that refuses crawlers made a decision, a site that renders only in JavaScript did not, and a site with clean HTML and no markup is one afternoon away from being fixed. Those carry different costs and different owners, so they are recorded separately. This is the whole set. There is no further reason and no free-text judgement of any site anywhere in this product.

Index of these pages: https://legibility.io/why

### js_shell: The content is assembled by JavaScript

URL: https://legibility.io/why/js_shell

The page arrived, but the facts on it are built in the browser after load. A crawler that does not run scripts sees an empty frame.

Shown to the site owner as: The page arrived, but its content is assembled by JavaScript. A crawler that does not run scripts sees an empty frame.

What is happening:
- The HTML came back successfully and contained almost no readable text: markup, script tags and a mount point, with the content fetched and rendered afterwards by the application.
- A browser does the remaining work and a person sees a complete page. A crawler that does not execute JavaScript sees what the server actually sent, which is close to nothing.
- This is the most common finding on modern commerce sites, and it is nearly always an accident of the framework rather than a decision anyone made.

What it costs:
- An assistant reading your product page finds no product. It will still answer the question it was asked, from whichever source it could read, which is usually a retailer carrying your item or a competitor carrying something close to it.
- The cost scales with how much of your catalogue is affected, which for a client-rendered site is normally all of it at once.
- It is also invisible in the usual places: nothing bounces, nothing times out, and no session is recorded, because the reader was never a session.

The fix: Serve the facts in the initial HTML response rather than assembling them after load. Server-side rendering, static generation, or a prerender layer for crawlers all achieve it. The test is simple: fetch your own page with curl and read what comes back.

Who does it: A frontend or platform engineer. Server-side rendering, static generation, or a prerender layer for crawlers all solve it. The test is one command: fetch your own page with curl and read what comes back.

### no_structured_data: The page has no structured data

URL: https://legibility.io/why/no_structured_data

The page reads fine as prose and carries nothing typed, so a machine has to infer what any of it means. Inference is where models invent things.

Shown to the site owner as: The page is readable as text but carries no structured data, so a machine has to guess what any of it means.

What is happening:
- The HTML came back, it contains real readable text, and it has no JSON-LD block and too few OpenGraph tags to work with.
- Everything on the page is available to a model only as prose it has to interpret. Which number is the price, whether that price is current, which of the words is the brand and which is the model, are all guesses.
- A guess that is right is indistinguishable from a guess that is wrong until someone acts on it.

What it costs:
- Your facts get restated approximately. Prices attach to the wrong variant, availability is asserted from a sentence that was true last quarter, and the brand name comes out as whatever appeared closest to the product name.
- Where a competitor on the same query does publish typed data, theirs is the version that can be stated with confidence, so theirs is the version that gets stated.

The fix: Add JSON-LD to the page. For a product that means a schema.org Product block carrying name, brand, price, currency and availability. It is one script tag in the head and it is the single highest-value change on this list.

Who does it: One script tag in the head, and whoever owns the page template can add it. A schema.org Product block carrying name, brand, price, currency and availability is the single highest-value change on this list.

### blocked: The site refused the request

URL: https://legibility.io/why/blocked

The server answered a plain request with a refusal rather than a page. That is a decision the site made, and it is often the right one.

Shown to the site owner as: The site refused the request. This is a choice the site made.

What is happening:
- A request arrived carrying an identified user agent and no browser fingerprint, and the server returned 401, 403 or 429, or a 200 whose body is a challenge page rather than the site. Either way nothing readable came back.
- This is usually a bot rule at a CDN or a firewall rather than a line someone wrote about this crawler specifically. Rules aimed at scrapers and credential stuffers catch every non-browser request, and an answer engine's crawler is a non-browser request.
- We record a refusal only when a second independent request path reproduces it. A single refusal that one client sees and another does not is recorded as inconclusive, because a refusal names a company and one client's word is not enough to publish that.

What it costs:
- If the refusal is intended, none. Choosing not to be read by machines is a legitimate position and plenty of publishers hold it deliberately.
- If it is not intended, it is the most complete version of the problem: an assistant asked about your products gets nothing at all and answers from a marketplace listing, a review aggregator or a competitor instead.
- Nothing about this appears in your analytics, because the request that failed was never a session and the visit that went elsewhere never happened.

The fix: If the refusal was intended, nothing needs fixing. If it was not, it usually comes from a bot rule or a firewall setting applied to all non-browser traffic rather than a decision about this crawler. Check what your CDN or WAF does with a plain server request that carries no browser fingerprint.

Who does it: Whoever owns the CDN or WAF configuration. Minutes to see what the rule does, longer to decide what you want it to do.

### low_confidence: The extraction did not clear the trust gate

URL: https://legibility.io/why/low_confidence

Typed data was there and something was extracted, but not well enough to rely on, so nothing is returned rather than something uncertain.

Shown to the site owner as: The page was read, but the extraction did not clear the 0.7 trust gate, so it is not safe to rely on.

What is happening:
- The extraction produced a result whose calibrated confidence landed below 0.7, which is the gate at which a read is treated as trustworthy.
- The usual causes are specific and fixable: a price with no currency attached, a product name that differs between the markup and the visible page, or several structured blocks on one page that disagree with each other.
- Below the gate the answer is withheld rather than returned with a caveat. A number that is probably right is worse than no number, because it gets used.

What it costs:
- You have done most of the work and are getting none of the benefit. The markup exists, and the disagreement inside it is enough to make the whole page unusable to anything that checks before it answers.
- Anything that does not check before it answers will use it anyway, which is the worse outcome of the two.

The fix: Structured data was present but incomplete or inconsistent enough that the extraction could not be relied on. The usual causes are a price without a currency, a name that differs between the markup and the visible page, or several conflicting blocks on one page.

Who does it: Whoever owns the product template. Usually a small correction rather than new work, because the markup is already there.

### robots_disallowed: robots.txt asked us not to read the page

URL: https://legibility.io/why/robots_disallowed

Your robots.txt disallows this crawler, so the page was never requested. That is recorded as a finding and never worked around.

Shown to the site owner as: robots.txt asks machines not to read this path. Recorded as a data point, never circumvented.

What is happening:
- robots.txt is fetched before anything else. When it disallows the path, no request for the page is made at all.
- Groups in robots.txt are not additive: the most specific matching group wins outright and the wildcard group is then ignored entirely. A rule written for one named crawler can silently stop applying to everything else, and the reverse.
- A disallow is published as a data point. Routing around it would make every number this product publishes worthless.

What it costs:
- If the rule was meant, none. Asking not to be read is a legitimate choice and we record it as a choice rather than a failure.
- If the rule was broader than intended, the cost is the same as a refusal: assistants answering questions about your products answer from somewhere else. A disallow aimed at one badly behaved scraper is often written in a way that covers every non-browser request, including the ones that would have cited you.

The fix: Nothing, unless the rule was broader than you meant. A disallow aimed at one badly behaved crawler is often written in a way that covers every non-browser request, including the ones answering questions about your products.

Who does it: Whoever owns robots.txt. Reading it carefully is most of the work, because the group precedence rule surprises people.

### not_a_product: The page is not a product page

URL: https://legibility.io/why/not_a_product

The page was read successfully. Nothing on it identifies it as a product, because it probably is not one.

Shown to the site owner as: The page was read successfully, but it is not a product page.

What is happening:
- The read worked and the markup carried no indication that this page describes something purchasable.
- For a homepage, a category listing, an article or an about page, that is correct and expected. The check requests one page, and on most sites that page is not a product page.
- Where it is wrong is a genuine product page whose markup does not say so, which reads to a machine exactly like a page about nothing in particular.

What it costs:
- For a page that is not a product, none at all. This is a description rather than a fault.
- For a product page that does not identify itself, the same cost as carrying no structured data: an assistant asked about that item does not find it here.

The fix: Nothing, if the page is not meant to be one. If it is a product page, the markup on it does not identify it as such, and adding a schema.org Product block is what closes that gap.

Who does it: Nothing, unless the page is meant to be a product. If it is, a schema.org Product block is what closes the gap.

### timeout: The page did not answer in time

URL: https://legibility.io/why/timeout

Twelve seconds passed without a response. No verdict about the markup is possible, because no markup arrived.

Shown to the site owner as: The page did not answer in time.

What is happening:
- The request was made and nothing came back within the budget. This is a statement about the response, not about the page.
- It can be transient. It can also be what a plain server request from a datacenter address consistently gets, when a browser from a residential one does not.
- Nothing is recorded about your structured data, because none of it was seen.

What it costs:
- Directly, only that this read produced nothing. Worth repeating before drawing any conclusion from it.
- Indirectly, it is worth knowing that most crawlers budget less time than twelve seconds. A page that takes that long here has already been abandoned by several of them.

The fix: The page did not answer within 12 seconds from a plain server request. Worth checking what your origin does under that condition, because a crawler with a shorter budget than ours would have given up sooner.

Who does it: Whoever watches origin response times. Start by checking what the origin does for an uncached request with no browser headers.

### error: The result was inconclusive

URL: https://legibility.io/why/error

Something went wrong that we cannot attribute to your site. We would rather say we do not know than publish a finding we cannot stand behind.

Shown to the site owner as: The result was inconclusive. We do not know, and we would rather say so.

What is happening:
- This covers the cases where the read failed for a reason that is not evidence about the page: an unexpected status, a connection that did not complete, or a refusal that one request path saw and a second did not.
- That last case is the important one. During development a plain request received 403 from two well-known newspapers while a different client received 200 and 302 from the same machine seconds apart. The difference was the HTTP client, not the sites. Recording the first would have published a false accusation against both.
- So when the evidence disagrees with itself, the verdict is this one rather than the more interesting one.

What it costs:
- None that can be established from this read. Anyone treating it as a problem with your site is reading more into it than it says.
- Run it again. If it settles into a specific finding, that finding is the one to act on.

The fix: Nothing yet. The result was inconclusive rather than bad, and the honest response to that is to read the page again rather than to report a finding we cannot stand behind.

Who does it: Nothing yet. The honest response to an inconclusive read is another read.

## Answers, in full

Each answer opens with the direct answer, then the detail and a short FAQ. Index: https://legibility.io/answers. Feed: https://legibility.io/answers/feed.xml.

### How can an AI agent get typed product data from a URL or a barcode?

URL: https://legibility.io/answers/how-can-an-ai-agent-get-typed-product-data-from-a-url-or-barcode
Published: 2026-10-21. Updated: 2026-10-21.

Call read_product with exactly one of a product url or a gtin barcode. Legibility returns a typed product object with a price band, per-field confidence, an overall calibrated confidence, the extraction method and the cost of the call. It is available over REST at /api/v1/read_product and as an MCP tool.

An agent that has to decide what to buy needs facts it can act on, not a page of HTML and a guess. A typed object with a confidence attached lets the agent check one number before acting, instead of trusting whatever a scraper happened to pull out.

#### A request that works today

The GTIN below is a real barcode that returns a trusted object:

```bash
curl -X POST https://legibility.io/api/v1/read_product \
  -H "authorization: Bearer lgk_your_key" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"gtin":"8076800195057"}'
```

A product URL works the same way with {"url":"https://..."}. Sending both, or neither, is rejected as an invalid request.

#### What comes back

```json
{
  "request_id": "req_...",
  "input": { "gtin": "8076800195057" },
  "product": {
    "title": "...",
    "brand": "...",
    "gtin": "...",
    "price": { "low": 110, "high": 110, "currency": "USD", "as_of": "...", "n_sources": 2 },
    "availability": "in_stock",
    "attributes": {}
  },
  "legibility_id": "pl_...",
  "field_confidence": { "title": 0.95, "price": 0.8 },
  "confidence": 0.77,
  "method": "gtin",
  "calibration_version": "...",
  "sources": ["..."],
  "cost_usd": 0.012,
  "cached": false,
  "as_of": "..."
}
```

- confidence is a calibrated probability, and 0.7 is the trust gate. See what a calibrated confidence means.
- price is a band with an as_of time and a source count, not a guaranteed live price.
- method names the path that produced the object: jsonld, shopify, opengraph, gtin, name or cache.
- legibility_id is a stable opaque id for a trusted product, safe to store as a foreign key.
- cost_usd is the cost of this call, stamped in the response.

#### What it can read today

Trusted coverage is structured, verifiable data: pages that serve JSON-LD schema.org/Product to a plain request, Shopify storefronts, barcode lookups, and OpenGraph product pages admitted through a verified prior. Retailers that block datacenter requests do not return a trusted object today. When a page cannot be read, the envelope is still well formed, with product: null and a confidence below the gate, and the reason pages explain each failure.

#### Billing for a keyed call

With an API key the billing unit is the trusted read: a call is billable only when it returns a product at confidence 0.7 or higher. A null or below-gate read is not billed and does not count against quota. The free plan includes 1,000 trusted reads a month with a hard stop. Over MCP an agent can also pay per call in USDC, as described in how an agent pays per call.

#### The related tools

- resolve_product takes a fuzzy name and returns the same envelope in the same call. There is no job id to poll.
- compare_products takes two to five URLs and returns a side-by-side matrix with the price delta. REST only.
- brief_product returns the typed object plus a short summary composed from its fields. REST only.

Request and response details are in the read_product reference and the quickstart.

FAQ:
- Q: What happens if the page cannot be read? A: The response has product: null and a confidence below 0.7. On an API key that read is free and does not use quota.
- Q: Is the price a live price? A: No. It is a band with low, high, currency, as_of and n_sources, because product-page prices are often stale, regional or promotional.
- Q: Can I send a URL and a GTIN together? A: No. read_product takes exactly one of them, and a request with both or neither is rejected before any work is done.

### How can an AI agent pay per API call in USDC?

URL: https://legibility.io/answers/how-can-an-ai-agent-pay-per-api-call-in-usdc
Published: 2026-10-21. Updated: 2026-10-21.

An agent pays per call in USDC with x402: it calls the API without a key, receives HTTP 402 with payment requirements, signs a USDC transfer authorization for the quoted amount, and resends the request with an X-PAYMENT header. Legibility's MCP server works this way today on Base Sepolia, a testnet, with no mainnet settlement yet.

x402 puts payment inside HTTP itself. There is no signup, no API key and no invoice: the payment header is the credential, and the server proves settlement in its response. That is what lets an agent find a tool and pay for it on its own.

#### How the flow works, step by step

1. Discover for free. On Legibility's MCP server, initialize, tools/list and ping cost nothing, so an agent can read the tools and their input schemas before deciding to pay.
2. Call without a key. A tools/call with no Authorization header and no X-PAYMENT header returns HTTP 402 with a JSON body: x402Version, an error string, and an accepts array of payment requirements.
3. Read the requirements. Each entry names the scheme (exact), the network (base-sepolia), maxAmountRequired in atomic USDC units (USDC has 6 decimals), the asset contract, the payTo address and maxTimeoutSeconds.
4. Sign and resend. The agent signs an ERC-3009 TransferWithAuthorization for that amount, which is gasless for the buyer, base64-encodes the payment payload and resends the same request with it in the X-PAYMENT header.
5. Settlement and result. Legibility verifies and then settles the payment through an x402 facilitator (by default https://x402.org/facilitator), runs the tool, and returns the result with an X-PAYMENT-RESPONSE header carrying the settlement proof.

#### What the 402 looks like

The first, unpaid call:

```bash
curl -i -X POST https://legibility.io/api/mcp \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_product","arguments":{"gtin":"8076800195057"}}}'
```

The response is HTTP 402 with a body shaped like this:

```json
{
  "x402Version": 1,
  "error": "Payment required: provide a lgk_ API key (Bearer) or a settled X-PAYMENT header.",
  "accepts": [
    {
      "scheme": "exact",
      "network": "base-sepolia",
      "maxAmountRequired": "10000",
      "resource": "https://legibility.io/api/mcp",
      "description": "Legibility read_product",
      "mimeType": "application/json",
      "payTo": "0x...",
      "maxTimeoutSeconds": 120,
      "asset": "0x036CbD53842c5426634e7929541eC2318f3dCF7e",
      "extra": { "name": "USDC", "version": "2" }
    }
  ]
}
```

Treat the quote you receive as authoritative rather than a number from documentation. The amount is server configuration; the default in Legibility's code is 10000 atomic units, which is 0.01 USDC. The asset shown is USDC on Base Sepolia.

#### What to know before relying on it

- Testnet only today. Settlement runs on Base Sepolia. The on-chain path is wired and testable, but no mainnet settlement is live yet.
- Payment settles before the read runs. On the x402 path the payment is verified and settled first, so a paid call that returns product: null has still been paid for. The rule that misses are free applies to API key billing, where only trusted reads count.
- Input validation is free. Malformed arguments, such as passing both url and gtin, come back as a tool error before any payment is requested.
- MCP only. x402 is accepted on the MCP endpoint at https://legibility.io/api/mcp. The REST endpoints under /api/v1 take an API key.
- No account metering. x402 calls are paid on-chain, so they skip account rate limiting and monthly quota. A settlement failure returns 402 again with a settle_error field.

#### The API key alternative

If a human sets the agent up, an API key may be simpler. Create an lgk_ key in the dashboard and send it as Authorization: Bearer lgk_.... The free plan includes 1,000 trusted reads a month with a hard stop, and a call that returns nothing trusted is not billed. Plans are listed on the home page, and the payment protocol is documented at MCP and x402.

FAQ:
- Q: Does an agent need an account to pay per call? A: No. With x402 the signed payment in the X-PAYMENT header is the credential. Discovery calls are free, and a paid tools/call needs no key and no signup.
- Q: Which network and token does Legibility accept? A: USDC on Base Sepolia, which is a testnet. The asset address is 0x036CbD53842c5426634e7929541eC2318f3dCF7e. Mainnet settlement is not live yet.
- Q: Is an x402 call charged when the read returns nothing? A: Yes. The payment settles before the read runs. With an API key the answer is different: only a trusted read, meaning a product returned at confidence 0.7 or higher, is billed.

### How do I connect an AI agent to a remote MCP server over HTTP?

URL: https://legibility.io/answers/how-do-i-connect-an-ai-agent-to-a-remote-mcp-server
Published: 2026-10-21. Updated: 2026-10-21.

Send JSON-RPC 2.0 requests by HTTP POST to the server's endpoint: initialize first, then tools/list to read the tool schemas, then tools/call to run one. Legibility's MCP server is at https://legibility.io/api/mcp, speaks protocol version 2025-06-18, and describes itself at /.well-known/mcp.json. Discovery is free.

The Model Context Protocol gives an agent one way to find out what a server can do and then do it. Over HTTP that is ordinary POST requests carrying JSON-RPC messages, so any client that can make an HTTP request can use it.

#### The three calls

Start the session. The server echoes the protocol version you send, or answers with 2025-06-18:

```bash
curl -X POST https://legibility.io/api/mcp \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -H "accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18"}}'
```

List the tools and their input schemas:

```bash
curl -X POST https://legibility.io/api/mcp \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list"}'
```

Call one. This needs an API key or an x402 payment:

```bash
curl -X POST https://legibility.io/api/mcp \
  -H "authorization: Bearer lgk_your_key" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"read_product","arguments":{"gtin":"8076800195057"}}}'
```

The tool result arrives as JSON-RPC result.content, a list with one text item holding the JSON response envelope.

#### What the server does with each message

- initialize returns capabilities: { tools: {} } and serverInfo naming the server.
- notifications/initialized is accepted with HTTP 202 and no body.
- ping returns an empty result, and tools/list returns the tools with their JSON Schemas.
- An unknown method returns JSON-RPC error -32601; an unknown tool name returns -32602; a body that is not JSON returns -32700.
- Bad tool arguments come back as a normal result with isError: true, so the agent sees why without the call failing at the transport level.
- Each POST gets one JSON response. A GET to the endpoint returns HTTP 405 with allow: POST.

#### Which tools are on the MCP server

Two, today: read_product (exactly one of url or gtin, plus an optional min_confidence) and resolve_product (a name of two or more characters). compare_products and brief_product exist over REST at /api/v1 but are not yet on the MCP tool list, and that is stated rather than implied.

#### Authentication and limits

A tools/call needs one of two things. Either an API key sent as Authorization: Bearer lgk_..., or an x402 payment in USDC sent as an X-PAYMENT header, which is explained in how an agent pays per call. Keyed calls are rate limited per plan: over the limit returns HTTP 429 with retry-after and JSON-RPC error -32099. A free account past its monthly quota receives HTTP 402 with error -32098 before any work is done.

#### Finding the server in the first place

An agent or a registry can read https://legibility.io/.well-known/mcp.json, which states the endpoint, the transport, that discovery is free, both auth methods, and the tool list. The same facts are in plain text at llms.txt, and the reference page is MCP and x402.

FAQ:
- Q: Is listing the tools free? A: Yes. initialize, tools/list and ping need no key and no payment. Only tools/call is paid.
- Q: Can I use a streaming or GET connection? A: No. The endpoint accepts POST only and answers each request with a single JSON response. A GET returns 405.
- Q: Why is compare_products missing from tools/list? A: It is REST only for now, as is brief_product. Both are available at /api/v1 with an API key.

### What does a calibrated confidence score mean when an agent reads product data?

URL: https://legibility.io/answers/what-does-a-calibrated-confidence-score-mean-for-an-agent
Published: 2026-10-21. Updated: 2026-10-21.

A calibrated confidence is a probability: a score of 0.7 means the result is about 70 percent likely to be correct. Legibility fits its scores with isotonic regression on a held-out labelled split and treats 0.7 as the trust gate, so an agent can decide to act, re-check or decline on a number that means something.

Most extraction tools return a score that measures how many fields were filled, or how sure a model sounded. Neither tells an agent how often results at that score are actually right, which is the only thing it needs to know before acting.

#### Calibrated versus uncalibrated

An uncalibrated score orders results but does not say how often they are correct. A calibrated score is fitted against labelled outcomes so that, across many results, the stated number matches the observed rate of being right. That is what makes a fixed threshold meaningful: "act at 0.7 or above" becomes a statement about expected error rather than a guess.

#### The measured figures, with their limits

Legibility's calibration was measured on a held-out test split of 63 labelled items, in evaluation run iso-63-2026-07-05:

- Precision at the 0.7 gate: 1.0, with a Wilson lower bound of 0.832.
- GTIN recall: 1.0. Adversarial rejection: 1.0.
- Expected calibration error across the full range: 0.19.

The honest reading is that the score is dependable at the gate and looser in the middle of the range. Sixty-three items is one evaluation run, which is a claim rather than a credential, so the sample size is published with the number. Every response carries calibration_version, so a stored score stays auditable after a recalibration.

#### How an agent should use it

1. Gate on confidence. At 0.7 or above the object is treated as trusted; below it, treat the read as unknown.
2. Use field_confidence when one field matters more than the rest, for example acting on the price only when the price field clears your own bar.
3. Adjust the gate with min_confidence (0 to 1) when your task tolerates more or less risk than the default.
4. Store legibility_id and calibration_version with any decision you make from the read.
5. Close the loop with report_outcome, which records whether the answer led to a real result and is never billed.

#### Why the gate is also the billing unit

With an API key, Legibility bills only trusted reads: a product returned at confidence 0.7 or higher. A miss or a below-gate read costs nothing and does not use quota. Charging for misses would reward the opposite of an honest gate. The method is described on the home page and in the read_product answer.

FAQ:
- Q: Can I change the 0.7 threshold? A: Yes. Pass min_confidence between 0 and 1 on read_product, resolve_product or brief_product, over REST or MCP.
- Q: Is the score equally reliable at every value? A: No. Expected calibration error across the full range is 0.19, so the score is most dependable at the gate and looser in the middle.
- Q: How large was the evaluation? A: A held-out test split of 63 items in one run. The figures are published with that sample size rather than as a headline alone.

### Why can't an AI agent read a product page?

URL: https://legibility.io/answers/why-cant-an-ai-agent-read-a-product-page
Published: 2026-10-21. Updated: 2026-10-21.

Because a plain request did not return typed facts a machine can extract without guessing. Legibility records which of eight reasons applies: a refusal, a JavaScript-only render, no structured data, not a product page, an extraction below the trust gate, a robots.txt disallow, a timeout, or an inconclusive read.

The distinction matters because the reasons have different causes and different owners. Refusing crawlers is a decision a site is entitled to make. Rendering only in JavaScript is usually an accident of how the site was built. A clean page with no markup is often a small fix.

#### What readable means here

A page is readable when typed facts can be extracted without guessing, which in practice means JSON-LD or OpenGraph. Legibility tests that with one plain GET of the page, the way an answer engine's crawler would issue it, using the identified user agent LegibilityBot/0.1. There is no headless browser, and no proxy is used to get around a refusal. robots.txt is obeyed, and a site that disallows the bot is recorded as having chosen to, never worked around.

#### The eight reasons

- blocked: the site refused the request.
- js_shell: the content is assembled by JavaScript, so the plain HTML carries little to read.
- no_structured_data: the page loads but carries no typed markup.
- not_a_product: what came back is not a product page.
- low_confidence: something was extracted, but it scored below the 0.7 trust gate.
- robots_disallowed: robots.txt asks machines not to read the page.
- timeout: the request did not complete in time.
- error: the read was inconclusive.

This is the whole set. Each page explains the mechanism, what it costs and who fixes it, and the index of findings orders them by cost.

#### What a site owner can do

Check one domain at legibility.io with no account to see which finding applies. Where the finding is a JavaScript-only render or missing structured data, serving schema.org/Product JSON-LD in the HTML response is the usual fix. Where the site has chosen to refuse machines, the finding is a decision rather than a defect, and it is reported that way.

#### What an agent can do with a failed read

A failed read_product still returns a well-formed envelope with product: null and a confidence below the gate, so the agent can branch on it instead of parsing an error. Options include trying the product's GTIN, which goes through barcode sources rather than the page, or resolving a name with resolve_product. With an API key a failed read is not billed. See how to get typed product data.

FAQ:
- Q: Does Legibility render JavaScript before deciding? A: No. It makes one plain request with no headless browser, because that is the request an answer engine crawler issues, and a page that needs JavaScript to show its facts is recorded as js_shell.
- Q: Does Legibility get around blocks or robots.txt? A: No. robots.txt is obeyed and a refusal is recorded as a finding. A proxy-based fallback exists for bot-hostile sites but is switched off.
- Q: Can I check my own site? A: Yes. Enter a domain at legibility.io and get a verdict with no account and no payment.

## About the crawler

LegibilityBot identifies itself on every request and the identifying URL resolves: https://legibility.io/about/bot. It makes one plain GET of the page, does not execute JavaScript, does not use a proxy or residential address to route around a refusal, submits nothing, and obeys robots.txt. A site that disallows it is recorded as having chosen to, never circumvented. Blocking instructions and a takedown route are on that page.
